analysis.one_liner: Requires corporations, unions, and Super PACs to disclose who funds their political ads.
analysis.headline: The Senate's campaign-spending disclosure bill drew 52 cosponsors and one committee hearing, but never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any corporation, labor union, tax-exempt group, or Super PAC that spends more than $10,000 on election ads to report that spending within 24 hours and to name donors who gave $10,000 or more. It would also expand the definition of political ads to cover messages that attack or support a candidate without saying "vote for" or "vote against," and extend the disclosure window to the entire election year rather than just the final weeks. The aim was to let voters see who is paying for the political ads they watch.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters benefit most: they would see, before casting a ballot, which corporations, unions, and wealthy donors paid for the ads aimed at them. Candidates and groups that already disclose their spending would also gain a more level playing field, since rivals could no longer run attack ads through intermediaries that never reveal their funders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want to know who funds ads

how_it_helps.text: It requires any corporation, union, tax-exempt group, or Super PAC spending more than $10,000 on campaign ads to report each payment and the identity of donors who gave $10,000 or more, filed within 24 hours during election season.

It closes the main gap courts and the FEC left open: ads that attack or boost a candidate without saying 'vote for' would count as election spending, and political ads would be covered for the entire election year, not just the final weeks.
It applies the same donor-disclosure rules to Super PAC accounts that accept unlimited donations, the channel used by billionaires and large interests that ordinary donors cannot use.
Statements would be filed under penalty of perjury, putting a named executive behind each report.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, tax-exempt advocacy groups, and Super PACs spending on elections would bear the compliance costs of rapid reporting and would lose the ability to run ads without naming their large donors. Donors giving $10,000 or more to political groups would be publicly identified.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate, union, and nonprofit ad spenders

drawbacks.text: Donors can avoid being named by putting their money in a segregated account and prohibiting its use for campaign ads, so some spending would stay anonymous even under the bill.
The disclosure duties fall on labor unions and nonprofit advocacy groups as well as corporations, and groups spending more than $10,000 would face rapid 24-hour reporting with penalties of perjury.
Publicly naming donors of $10,000 or more can expose supporters of controversial causes to harassment or retaliation — the standard objection to sweeping donor disclosure.
The bill repeals the ban on political contributions by individuals age 17 or younger, an unrelated change riding along with the disclosure provisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: voters would learn before an election who paid for the ads trying to sway them, closing the gap left when unlimited spending became legal. The costs are donor privacy — supporters of unpopular or controversial causes could face harassment or retaliation once named — and compliance work for advocacy groups. The bill also has design weaknesses an honest supporter would acknowledge: donors can stay unnamed by forbidding use of their money for campaign ads, and the rider repealing the ban on contributions by 17-year-olds has nothing to do with disclosure. On balance the disclosure benefit to voters outweighs the privacy cost, but the loopholes limit how much light it would actually cast.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in June 2014 and sent to the Senate Rules Committee, which held one hearing in July; the committee never voted on it and the Senate never brought it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 24, 2014, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration.
It drew 51 cosponsors — 49 Democrats and 2 independents — with no Republican support.
The Rules Committee held a single hearing on July 23, 2014, printed as S.Hrg. 113-610.
After the hearing, no further action was taken: no committee vote, no floor vote, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Groups that spend on elections without naming their donors — corporations, unions, and tax-exempt nonprofits — kept that anonymity, since no disclosure rule took effect; voters never got to see who paid for the ads.

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 51 cosponsors; it received one committee hearing and no vote.

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or independent — 50 Democrats plus 2 independents — with no Republican support, and the Senate (where Democrats held the majority) never voted on the bill.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt 'dark money' nonprofits (501(c)(4) and similar groups)
industries.note: These groups exist largely to run political ads without naming donors; the bill would force them to disclose donors of $10,000 or more, ending the anonymity that makes them attractive to large givers. Voters would learn who is behind the ads.

Super PACs would have to disclose the money moving through accounts that accept unlimited donations. Their fundraising advantage depends on scale that ordinary donors cannot match, and the bill sheds light on it.

Corporate political spending would carry the same 24-hour disclosure and donor naming rules. Executives would have to certify under penalty of perjury that spending was not coordinated with candidates.

Unions would face the same disclosure and compliance duties as corporations, losing the ability to spend on politics anonymously. Unlike corporate dark money, union political spending draws from member dues, so its interest in anonymity is more about privacy and paperwork than concealing influence from the public.
